questions.q: What changes, and what stays the same, when PPO is applied to a chain-of-thought reasoning trace instead of a short RLHF response?
options: Everything changes; PPO cannot be used on reasoning traces at all

The underlying RL machinery (policy, token-level actions, the clipped surrogate objective) stays the same; what changes is the content of the rollout, which is now a full reasoning trace plus final answer
Only the learning rate needs to change
The value function is no longer needed
questions.explain: A CoT trace is still just a trajectory of token-level actions scored and optimized with the same PPO mechanics from Chapter 4 — only the content being generated is longer and more structured.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the reward attachment points described in this lesson?
options: A single scalar reward on the whole trace
A scalar tied to the final answer's correctness
A score at each intermediate reasoning step
A reward computed by averaging the token count of the trace
questions.explain: The three attachment points covered are whole-trace scalar, outcome (final-answer) correctness, and per-step process reward — not a reward based on trace length.

questions.q: Why does this lesson argue that a Chapter 6-style learned preference reward model is a weak fit for scoring reasoning traces?
options: Because reward models cannot process long text
Because humans are slow and unreliable at checking dense reasoning like algebra, making preference labels noisy, expensive, and prone to rewarding confident-sounding but incorrect reasoning
Because reward models only work with images
Because Bradley-Terry models require exactly two annotators
questions.explain: Human preference judgment is a weaker proxy for correctness in dense reasoning than it is for style or helpfulness, so the resulting reward model can reward fluent wrongness.

questions.q: What property of math and code problems motivates moving away from a learned reward model toward a verifier-based reward?
options: Math and code problems are always short
Math and code have an objective, mechanically checkable notion of correctness — a final answer can be checked against a known solution, or code run against unit tests
Math and code problems never require reasoning
Verifiers are cheaper to train than any reward model
questions.explain: Because correctness in math and code can be checked programmatically, a rule-based verifier can replace a learned, subjective reward model — the premise behind RLVR, covered in lesson 55.

questions.q: In the lesson's rollout pseudocode, at which point does the reward signal enter the PPO update?
options: Before the trace is generated
After the trace is generated, via a score() call, which then feeds into advantage estimation and the PPO update
Reward is never used in this pseudocode
Only during tokenizer initialization
questions.explain: The pseudocode generates the full trace first, computes reward via score(prompt, trace), then computes the advantage and performs the PPO update — exactly mirroring the Chapter 4 PPO loop.
